extracted.intended_audience: federal judges, patent litigators, and jurors
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent trials setting forth legal standards and guidance on claim construction, infringement, validity, equitable defenses, and damages to be given to juries in U.S. federal patent litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: WHAT A PATENT IS AND HOW ONE IS OBTAINED
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanation of what a patent is (exclusive right granted by the U.S. PTO for a term) and the parts of a patent (specification, drawings, claims) and that it is granted after examination (prosecution history).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines patent, term, parts, prosecution history; explains that when patent expires invention dedicated to public.

rubrics_metrics.name: SUMMARY OF CONTENTIONS
rubrics_metrics.description: A preliminary summary instruction presenting the parties' contentions about infringement, validity, and other claims so the jury understands what issues will be tried.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to orient the jury to the parties' positions; not substantive law but procedural overview.

rubrics_metrics.name: PATENT AT ISSUE
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction identifying the specific patent(s) asserted in the case and the claims in controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tells jurors which patent(s) and claim(s) they must consider; may include reference to patent numbers and claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: OVERVIEW OF APPLICABLE LAW
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary instruction summarizing the legal concepts that will govern the trial (e.g., burden of proof, claim construction, standards for infringement and invalidity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides jurors the legal framework they must apply when evaluating evidence presented at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: OUTLINE OF TRIAL
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary explanation of the sequence of trial events (opening statements, presentation of evidence, witnesses, closing arguments, jury instructions, deliberations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps jurors follow the courtroom process and understand when and how they will be instructed and asked to deliberate.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE ROLE OF THE CLAIMS OF A PATENT
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction that the patent's claims define the invention and the boundaries of the patentee's rights; the jury must compare the accused product/practice to the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the claims, not the specification in isolation, define what is protected; claims function like a boundary description.

rubrics_metrics.name: HOW A CLAIM DEFINES WHAT IT COVERS
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction describing that each patent claim is a requirement-by-requirement statement and that infringement requires that the accused product or method satisfies each limitation of a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains 'reads on'/'reads into' language: a claim 'reads on' a device when each required part is found in the device or method.

rubrics_metrics.name: INDEPENDENT AND DEPENDENT CLAIMS
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction explaining the difference between independent claims (stand alone) and dependent claims (refer to and incorporate another claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that a dependent claim incorporates the limitations of the claim to which it refers.

rubrics_metrics.name: CLAIM INTERPRETATION
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction regarding how to interpret claim language (the meaning of claim terms) using intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) and extrinsic evidence as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directs jurors that definitions given in the instructions control and explains that some terms may have special meaning in the patent's context; references case law (e.g., Phillips/Markman).

rubrics_metrics.name: SECTION 112, PARAGRAPH 6 (MEANS-PLUS-FUNCTION)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction on treatment of claim elements governed by 35 U.S.C. § 112, ¶ 6 (means-plus-function claim limitations), including how to identify corresponding structure in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that for such limitations, the claim covers the corresponding structure described in the specification and equivalents, and instructs jurors on how to apply that rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: INFRINGEMENT GENERALLY
rubrics_metrics.description: Overview instruction defining infringement and the different types (direct, induced, contributory) and that infringement requires performing all claim limitations either literally or under the doctrine of equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that to prove infringement the patentee must show by a preponderance of the evidence that the accused product/practice meets each claim limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: DIRECT INFRINGEMENT BY 'LITERAL INFRINGEMENT'
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction that literal infringement occurs when the accused product or method contains every requirement (limitation) of a claim exactly as claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If even one limitation is missing or different, there is no literal infringement of that claim; jury instructed to compare claim limitations to the accused device/method.

rubrics_metrics.name: LITERAL INFRINGEMENT OF SECTION 112, PARAGRAPH 6 CLAIM REQUIREMENTS
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction addressing literal infringement for means-plus-function limitations: requires that the accused device include the structure in the specification corresponding to the claimed function (or an equivalent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how to determine whether accused device performs the claimed function using the disclosed structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: DIRECT INFRINGEMENT 'UNDER THE DOCTRINE OF EQUIVALENTS'
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction that infringement can be found if the accused product/method performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to obtain the same result as the claimed limitation, even if not literally identical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides jury guidance on applying the doctrine of equivalents and highlights the tests and boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIMITATIONS ON DOCTRINE OF EQUIVALENTS
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction describing limits on the doctrine of equivalents (e.g., prosecution history estoppel, particularized tests), and that it cannot be used to cover subject matter surrendered during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains circumstances where DOE is barred or narrowed by prior claim amendments or disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: INDIRECT INFRINGEMENT—ACTIVE INDUCEMENT
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction that inducement requires proof that the accused infringer knowingly induced another to infringe and possessed specific intent to encourage infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directs jurors to consider evidence of intent, actions taken to encourage infringement, and knowledge of the patent and infringing nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: INDIRECT INFRINGEMENT—CONTRIBUTORY INFRINGEMENT
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction that contributory infringement occurs when a party sells or offers to sell a component specially made or adapted for use in an infringing device, knowing it is especially made for infringement and not a staple article of commerce suitable for substantial noninfringing use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the knowledge and non-staple use requirements and burden on plaintiff to prove these elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: INFRINGEMENT THROUGH SUPPLY OF COMPONENTS FROM U.S. FOR COMBINATION ABROAD
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction on infringement liability when components are supplied from the United States for combination abroad in a manner that would infringe if performed in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains statutory framework and elements required to find liability for such supply; see relevant case law references.

rubrics_metrics.name: INFRINGEMENT BY SALE/OFFER/USE/IMPORTATION OF PRODUCT MADE OUTSIDE U.S. BY PATENTED PROCESS
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction addressing infringement issues for products made abroad by a patented process and brought into the United States (liability for importation/sale/use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains applicable statutory rules and distinctions for process-patent-related infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: DIRECT INFRINGEMENT: COMPONENTS LOCATED OUTSIDE UNITED STATES
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction dealing with allegations that one or more components of a claimed system are located outside the United States and whether combined acts constitute infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains spatial/jurisdictional limits on direct infringement and applicable law on multi-component systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: DIRECT INFRINGEMENT: ACTS OF MULTIPLE PARTIES MUST BE COMBINED
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction that to find direct infringement when multiple parties perform steps, plaintiff must show that a single party exercised control or direction such that all steps are attributable to that party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References law governing joint and divided infringement and how jurors should evaluate proof that acts are attributable to one defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: INDIRECT INFRINGEMENT: ACCUSED PRACTICES SOME STEPS AND ANOTHER PRACTICES REMAINING STEPS
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction regarding liability when the accused performs some claim steps and another party performs remaining steps—distinguishes direct vs indirect infringement and when inducement/contributory liability applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains when combination of acts across parties may result in liability and evidentiary requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: INDIRECT INFRINGEMENT: ACCUSED ALLEGEDLY INDUCES OTHERS TO COLLECTIVELY PRACTICE ALL CLAIMED STEPS
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction that inducement liability can arise if the accused induces others to collectively perform all claim steps and had requisite knowledge and intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details proof required of intent and knowledge and evidence showing inducement of collective performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: WILLFUL INFRINGEMENT
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction on willfulness: acts of infringement that are objectively reckless or undertaken with willful blindness/subjective intent to infringe, potentially supporting enhanced damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains legal standards for willfulness, including objective/subjective components and authorities; describes consequences (enhanced damages) and the jury's role in assessing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: INVALIDITY—BURDEN OF PROOF
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction that a party (typically accused infringer) asserting invalidity bears the burden of proving invalidity by clear and convincing evidence (unless statute or case law provides otherwise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies standard of proof and how jurors should apply it when considering invalidity defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: WRITTEN DESCRIPTION REQUIREMENT
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction describing the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112: specification must show that inventor had possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how to evaluate sufficiency of written description and what evidence supports or undermines it.

rubrics_metrics.name: ENABLEMENT
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction that the patent specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides factors for evaluating enablement (undue experimentation) and directs jurors on relevant evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: BEST MODE
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction explaining the best mode requirement: if inventor knew a best mode of carrying out the invention at filing, it must be disclosed in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes legal consequences and how jurors should assess claims that best mode was not disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRIOR ART
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction defining prior art as previously known subject matter (issued patents, publications, public knowledge) relevant to novelty and obviousness analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains what counts as prior art and how jurors should treat documentary and testimonial evidence about prior availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: ANTICIPATION
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction that a claim is anticipated (invalid for lack of novelty) if a single prior art reference discloses every limitation of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directs jurors to compare claim limitations to the prior art reference and apply the standard for anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: OBVIOUSNESS
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction that a claim is invalid for obviousness if, considering the level of ordinary skill in the art, scope and content of prior art, and differences between prior art and claimed invention, the claimed invention would have been obvious at the time of invention/filer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes the Graham factors and sub-instructions: (i) level of ordinary skill, (ii) scope and content of the prior art, (iii) differences between claimed invention and prior art; also explains combination of references and secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others).

rubrics_metrics.name: LEVEL OF ORDINARY SKILL
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction on how to determine the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art for purposes of obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists relevant considerations (education, experience of practitioners, types of problems encountered, sophistication of technology) and how jurors should assess expert testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: SCOPE AND CONTENT OF THE PRIOR ART
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction directing jurors to identify the scope and content of the prior art relevant to the claimed invention when performing obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how to consider disclosures, teachings, and differences among prior art references.

rubrics_metrics.name: INVENTORSHIP
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction addressing the requirement that inventors be correctly named and issues related to joint inventorship or incorrect inventorship affecting validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains standards for determining who is an inventor and consequences of incorrect inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: INEQUITABLE CONDUCT
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction on inequitable conduct as an equitable defense: whether the patentee, with intent to deceive, withheld or misrepresented material information to the PTO such that the patent should be unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains elements (materiality and intent to deceive) and burden/standard of proof for inequitable conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: LACHES
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction that laches (undue and unreasonable delay in instituting suit causing material prejudice to defendant) is an equitable defense to certain relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains elements jurors must find to apply laches and its effect on remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: EQUITABLE ESTOPPEL
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction that equitable estoppel bars a patentee from asserting a patent where the patentee's conduct misled the alleged infringer to change position to its detriment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains elements (misleading conduct, reliance, prejudice) and consequences for relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROSECUTION LACHES
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction on prosecution laches: delay during patent prosecution that may render the patent unenforceable for delay-related prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes assessment of delay and prejudice to determine whether prosecution laches applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: UNCLEAN HANDS
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction that the patentee may be barred from relief if the patentee engaged in inequitable or unconscionable behavior connected to the subject matter of the suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the equitable doctrine and evidence that may support it.

rubrics_metrics.name: DAMAGES—INTRODUCTION
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction introducing patent damages principles: compensation for infringement, available forms (lost profits or reasonable royalty), and that damages must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that damages aim to make the patentee whole and that speculative awards are not permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: LOST PROFITS—'BUT FOR' TEST
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction that lost profits are measured by what the patentee would have earned but for the infringement, using established tests and evidentiary components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains factors and sub-elements used to prove lost profits, including demand, absence of acceptable noninfringing substitutes, patentee's manufacturing/selling capacity, and amount of profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: LOST PROFITS—DEMAND
rubrics_metrics.description: Subcriterion: the patentee must show demand for the patented product (that customers would have bought the patentee's product but for the infringement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how to evaluate market evidence showing demand existed and was for the patented features.

rubrics_metrics.name: LOST PROFITS—NONINFRINGING SUBSTITUTES—ACCEPTABILITY
rubrics_metrics.description: Subcriterion: the patentee must show that there were no acceptable noninfringing substitutes that customers would have purchased instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how jurors evaluate acceptability of substitutes to customers based on evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: LOST PROFITS—NONINFRINGING SUBSTITUTES—AVAILABILITY
rubrics_metrics.description: Subcriterion: the patentee must show that noninfringing substitutes were not available in sufficient quantity or at suitable terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directs jurors to consider availability and capacity of substitutes in the market.

rubrics_metrics.name: LOST PROFITS—CAPACITY
rubrics_metrics.description: Subcriterion: the patentee must demonstrate it had the capacity (or could have had) to make and sell the lost units during the damages period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains evidence that supports or undermines capacity claims (factory capacity, supply chain, ramp-up feasibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: LOST PROFITS—AMOUNT OF PROFIT
rubrics_metrics.description: Subcriterion: damages measured by the amount of profit the patentee would have made on the lost sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains calculation approaches and evidence used to estimate profits (margins, costs, accounting records).

rubrics_metrics.name: LOST PROFITS—MARKET SHARE
rubrics_metrics.description: Subcriterion: may consider patentee's market share in proving lost profits where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how market share evidence can factor into lost profit calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: LOST PROFITS—COLLATERAL SALES
rubrics_metrics.description: Subcriterion: patentee may recover profits from collateral sales generated by the patented product (sales of other products promoted by the patented product).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains when convoyed or derivative sales are compensable and how to assess them.

rubrics_metrics.name: LOST PROFITS—PRICE EROSION
rubrics_metrics.description: Subcriterion: damages may account for price erosion (downward pressure on price caused by infringement) affecting patentee's profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains evidence needed to attribute price erosion to infringement and how to measure it.

rubrics_metrics.name: REASONABLE ROYALTY—ENTITLEMENT
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction that if lost profits are not available or appropriate, a patentee is entitled to a reasonable royalty as compensation for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains conceptual basis: payment that would have resulted from a hypothetical negotiation prior to infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: REASONABLE ROYALTY—DEFINITION
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction defining reasonable royalty as the payment that would have resulted from a hypothetical negotiation between a willing licensor and willing licensee at the time infringement began.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes hypothetical negotiation framework; royalty is not limited to actual licenses unless relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: REASONABLE ROYALTY—RELEVANT FACTORS (GEORGIA-PACIFIC FACTORS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction listing factors to consider in determining a reasonable royalty — the so-called Georgia-Pacific factors (a non-exhaustive list of considerations for the hypothetical negotiation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Lists the factors (verbatim from the instructions):
1. The royalties received by the patentee for licensing the patent-in-suit.
2. The rates paid for use of other patents comparable to the patent-in-suit.
3. The nature and scope of the license (exclusive/nonexclusive; territorial restrictions).
4. The licensor's policy and marketing program to maintain monopoly by limiting licenses.
5. The commercial relationship between licensor and licensee (competitors, inventor/promoter).
6. The effect of selling the patented specialty in promoting sales of other products of the licensee (derivative or convoyed sales).
7. The duration of the patent and the term of the license.
8. The established profitability, commercial success, and popularity of the product made under the patents.
9. The utility and advantages of the patented property over old modes/devices.
10. The nature of the patented invention, the character of the commercial embodiment, and benefits to users.
11. The extent to which the infringer has made use of the invention and evidence probative of the value of that use.
12. The portion of the profit or selling price customary to allow for use of the invention in comparable businesses.
13. The portion of realizable profits credited to the invention vs nonpatented elements, processes, business risks, or improvements added by infringer.
14. The opinion and testimony of qualified experts.
15. The amount the licensor and licensee would have agreed upon in a hypothetical negotiation at the time infringement began.

Also instructs jurors that no single factor is dispositive, they may consider other relevant factors, and the final factor establishes the hypothetical negotiation framework. Committee comments note Georgia-Pacific origin and relevant case law (Uniloc, ResQNet, Lucent, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: DATE OF COMMENCEMENT OF DAMAGES—PRODUCTS
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction that damages commence on the date the alleged infringer both infringed and was notified of the alleged infringement, with marking rules and alternatives explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides alternatives: agreed date; if patentee sells a patented product, whether it 'marked' substantially all products with patent number (constructive notice); burden on patentee to prove marking compliance; if not marked, damages begin on date of actual notice (e.g., when complaint filed) if proven. Notes special rule for method claims (no notice requirement; damages begin as of patent issue date or infringement date, whichever is earlier). References 35 U.S.C. § 287 and case law (Crystal Semiconductor, Maxwell, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: GLOSSARY—TERMS CONTROLLING JURY DELIBERATIONS
rubrics_metrics.description: Glossary definitions of technical and legal terms (e.g., abstract, embodiment, enablement, claim, limitation, prior art, specification) that must be followed and control deliberations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides short definitions to ensure jurors use consistent meanings; instructs that glossary and instruction definitions control over other characterizations.
